tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

---
name: dev-layout-and-discovery
description: "How DEV projects must be laid out to stay visible to KeystoneOS discovery, and the gitignored-subtree trap that silently voids backups"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: ea41d487-7812-4180-a6a8-f76a99753f83
  modified: 2026-11-02T23:17:20.641Z
---

Each project gets its own folder in `~/DEV`. KeystoneOS is a map and
control plane, not a monorepo — it maps projects by reference and never holds
their source (`AGENTS.md` operating rules).

**Depth limit.** `data/discovery-roots.json` scans `~/DEV` at `maxDepth 2`,
so `DEV/Project` and `DEV/Group/Project` are discovered but `DEV/Group/Sub/Project`
is invisible to `keystone.ps1 inventory` — it still works as code, it just never
appears in the registry or dashboard. One level of grouping (e.g. `Football\`) is
safe; two is not.

**The trap worth remembering:** never put a project under a path whose whole
subtree is gitignored. On 2026-07-28 two real projects were found living in
`KeystoneOS/outputs/`, which `.gitignore` covers with `outputs/**`. 53 of their 54
files existed only on one laptop, including files edited three weeks earlier. The
gitignore was correct for generated output; the mistake was storing source there.
The folder that looked most "inside the system" was the least protected thing in
the repo.

**Concurrency caveat.** Agent sessions (Claude and Codex) commit to DEV repos
while you are reading them — `SportScienceResearchRepo` moved HEAD and dropped
from 47 dirty files to 0 mid-analysis on 2026-07-28. Re-verify git numbers at the
point you act on them, not from a scan taken minutes earlier.

The root's display name in that config is still the Windows-era string
"Desktop DEV" — a label, not a path. The `path` field is `/Users/kristinarash/DEV`.

**Area folders (2026-11-02).** Repos now sit one level down in `~/DEV/{Personal,Program,Research,Performance}/`
(64 moved); `Football/` was already grouped. Still at the top until the after-season Workflow run: Platform repos
(KeystoneOS, project-triage, claude-global-memory, drive-tools...), `SpecialRequests`, `LibraryProject`, 3 live
pipelines, 4 repos in no router. Before moving a repo: grep consumers for `DEV/<name>` AND `"DEV" / "<name>"` and
`parents[n] / "<name>"`; rebuild any `.venv` (absolute paths); rename its Tier A slug folder; update
`portfolio.json` `dev_folder` and `KeystoneOS/data/projects.json` (UTF-8 BOM). Steps: `~/DEV/docs/FILE-ORGANIZATION-PLAN.md` Task 4.

description: "How DEV projects must be laid out to stay visible to KeystoneOS discovery, and the gitignored-subtree trap that silently voids backups"
metadata:

Each project gets its own folder in `~/DEV`. KeystoneOS is a map and
control plane, not a monorepo — it maps projects by reference and never holds
their source (`AGENTS.md` operating rules).

**Depth limit.** `data/discovery-roots.json` scans `~/DEV` at `maxDepth 2`,
so `DEV/Project` and `DEV/Group/Project` are discovered but `DEV/Group/Sub/Project`
is invisible to `keystone.ps1 inventory` — it still works as code, it just never
appears in the registry or dashboard. One level of grouping (e.g. `Football\`) is
safe; two is not.

**The trap worth remembering:** never put a project under a path whose whole
subtree is gitignored. On 2026-07-28 two real projects were found living in
`KeystoneOS/outputs/`, which `.gitignore` covers with `outputs/**`. 53 of their 54
files existed only on one laptop, including files edited three weeks earlier. The
gitignore was correct for generated output; the mistake was storing source there.
The folder that looked most "inside the system" was the least protected thing in
the repo.

**Concurrency caveat.** Agent sessions (Claude and Codex) commit to DEV repos
while you are reading them — `SportScienceResearchRepo` moved HEAD and dropped
from 47 dirty files to 0 mid-analysis on 2026-07-28. Re-verify git numbers at the
point you act on them, not from a scan taken minutes earlier.

The root's display name in that config is still the Windows-era string
"Desktop DEV" — a label, not a path. The `path` field is `/Users/kristinarash/DEV`.

**Area folders (2026-11-02).** Repos now sit one level down in `~/DEV/{Personal,Program,Research,Performance}/`
(64 moved); `Football/` was already grouped. Still at the top until the after-season Workflow run: Platform repos
(KeystoneOS, project-triage, claude-global-memory, drive-tools...), `SpecialRequests`, `LibraryProject`, 3 live
pipelines, 4 repos in no router. Before moving a repo: grep consumers for `DEV/<name>` AND `"DEV" / "<name>"` and
`parents[n] / "<name>"`; rebuild any `.venv` (absolute paths); rename its Tier A slug folder; update
`portfolio.json` `dev_folder` and `KeystoneOS/data/projects.json` (UTF-8 BOM). Steps: `~/DEV/docs/FILE-ORGANIZATION-PLAN.md` Task 4.

# /project: portfolio registry

Drives the `project-triage` CLI. The registry, `portfolio.json`, is the single
source of truth; each repo's `docs/STATUS.md` holds its tasks, which the board
reads only.

## Paths

- `$PT` is the folder holding `portfolio_json` in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json`.
  On the Mac that is `~/DEV/project-triage`: start each Bash call with
  `PT=~/DEV/project-triage` (the shell does not keep it between calls).
- Interpreter: `python3` on the Mac (there is no `python`). On Windows, use `python` and the
  `portfolio_json` folder from `config.windows.json` wherever this skill says `python3` and `$PT`.
- `portfolio.py` makes every change and always writes the live `$PT/portfolio.json` (only
  the read commands take `--registry`). `board.py` serves the board.

## CLI

```
python3 "$PT/portfolio.py" add-idea "<pitch>" --source "<source>"
python3 "$PT/portfolio.py" add-update "<name>" "<note>" [--next-action "<step>"]
python3 "$PT/portfolio.py" set-stage "<name>" "<stage>"
python3 "$PT/portfolio.py" set-status "<name>" active|paused|done [--note "<note>"]
python3 "$PT/portfolio.py" set-receiver "<name>" "<who, or me: why>"
python3 "$PT/board.py" --background
```

| Command | Prints on success |
|---|---|
| `add-idea` | `idea captured (<N> in inbox)` |
| `add-update` | `updated <name>` |
| `set-stage` | `stage set: <name> → <stage>` |
| `set-status` | `status set: <name> → <status>` |
| `set-receiver` | `<Name>: receiver <who>` |
| `board.py --background` | `board started at <url>` or `board already running at <url>` |

- Pass each name exactly as `projects[].name` spells it: `set-status` matches case-sensitively.
  Stages, in ladder order: `idea grilled spec planned building shipped`.
- `set-status active` on a row that was not active stamps `started` and renumbers the lane.
- A refused change prints `[error] <msg>` to stderr, exits 2 and leaves `portfolio.json`
  unchanged; a bad argument prints argparse usage and also exits 2. `board.py` prints
  `board did not start; see <log>` (exit 1), or a traceback when the registry fails to load.
  On any non-zero exit: stop and show the output verbatim.

## Ideas land in the board's Inbox

`add-idea` writes a card to the registry's `inbox` list, the board's Inbox column (since
2026-10-31; the older `ideas` list is history only). The card's name is `--name`, or the
pitch's first four words, made `[A-Za-z0-9_]` and suffixed `_2`, `_3` to stay unique. It
prints `idea captured as <Name> (<N> in the board inbox)`: tell Eric the card name and that
dragging it onto a lane, or `/project promote <Name>`, starts it.

## Verbs

**Name matching** (every verb that takes `<name>`): read `portfolio.json` and match the name
against `projects[].name`. One clear match: use that exact name. Several or none: ask Eric
which project before running anything.

### `idea <pitch>`
`add-idea "<pitch>" --source "<where it came from, ≤8 words>" --name <Short_Name>`, e.g.
`--source "chat about GPS vendor gaps"` (a place, not just "chat"). Pick `--name` as the
2–4 word project name the idea would get (`GPS_Vendor_Gaps`); it becomes the DEV folder name
on promotion.

### `update <name> <note>`
`add-update "<name>" "<note>"`, plus `--next-action "<step>"` when Eric gave one.

### `start` / `park` / `done <name>`
`set-status "<name>" active|paused|done`, with `--note` when Eric gave a reason. Starting a
`job`, `side` or `tool` row with no `receiver`: ask Eric who it is for, then run
`set-receiver` with his words (`me: <why>` when it is for himself).
On `start` (and after `promote`), check the project NAME for a person's name, an athlete,
a recruit or a health term (RTP, injury, women's health, DEXA...). None: run
`portfolio.py decide <name> phone-ok --source "Claude name check <date>"` so the phone page
shows it. Any, or unsure: leave it; the phone page shows "Project #n" instead.

### `stage <name> <stage>`
`set-stage "<name>" "<stage>"`. When the stage is `shipped`, offer once: "Want me to run
/harvest on <name> to distill it into your SecondBrain and log the shipped artifact?" On
yes, invoke the `harvest` skill for that project.

### `promote <idea>` and `rank`
Both change the registry where no CLI command reaches: follow
[`REGISTRY-EDITS.md`](REGISTRY-EDITS.md). Dragging cards on the board re-ranks faster.

### bare `/project`
Run `board.py --background` and give the URL. Waiting ideas are the board's Inbox column.

## After a change

The board picks up registry changes on its next poll (a few seconds); there is nothing to
render. Tell Eric in one line what changed. Closeout commits the registry as
`data: board edits <date>`, so leave `portfolio.json` uncommitted unless Eric asks.

Delete a project or idea only after Eric confirms that exact row.

**Done when:** the command printed its success line (or the hand edit saved and the
`.bak` beside `portfolio.json` was refreshed), and Eric has the one-line summary.

# Registry edits with no CLI command

`promote` and `rank` change `portfolio.json` through `portfolio.load_registry` /
`save_registry`, run from `$PT` (see SKILL.md, Paths). Use these functions, not the Edit
tool: `save_registry` validates the whole file first, refreshes `portfolio.json.bak` the
way the CLI and the board do (the provenance check in Tier A memory reads it), and
replaces the file atomically while the board polls it. Load, change and save in one
script, as below, so a board edit has well under a second to land in between.

A refused save raises `RegistryError: <problems>` and leaves the file unchanged: show it
verbatim and stop.

## promote `<idea>`

Dragging an Inbox card onto a lane does the same thing on the board.

1. Find the card: `inbox[]` rows whose `name` matches (or whose `purpose` matches Eric's
   words). One match, or ask Eric which.
2. Ask Eric for the lane (`job`, `side`, `system`, `knowledge`, `tool`) and the next action.
   Keep the card's `purpose` unless he gives a shorter one.
3. Promote with the board's own function, `board_ops.promote`: it refuses a name that is
   already a project, lands the row `active` at stage `idea` with `started` stamped, ranks
   it (position 0 is the top of its stage column), and removes the card from the inbox.

```
cd "$PT" && python3 - <<'EOF'
from pathlib import Path
import portfolio as pf, board_ops
p = Path("portfolio.json"); d = pf.load_registry(p)
name = "<Card_Name>"
rec = next(r for r in d["inbox"] if r["name"] == name)
board_ops.promote(d, name, "<lane>", "idea", 0, rec.get("purpose", ""), "<next action>")
pf.save_registry(p, d)
print("promoted", name, board_ops.find(d, name)["rank"])
EOF
```

4. A `job`, `side` or `tool` row also gets a receiver: the start step in SKILL.md.

## rank

The board shows each lane as stage columns (an `unstaged` column, then `idea` → `shipped`),
and `rank` orders the cards within a column. Board drags and card edits renumber the lane
stage by stage. So a rank order holds only within a stage.

1. Show the lane's active rows grouped by stage, in current `rank` order, and ask Eric for
   his order. If his order crosses stages, tell him the stage grouping wins.
2. Apply exactly his order: his rows take temporary ranks below 1 in that order, then the
   board's own renumbering (`_renumber`, which also numbers the lane's paused rows) gives
   every row its final rank:

```
cd "$PT" && python3 - <<'EOF'
from pathlib import Path
import portfolio as pf, board_ops
p = Path("portfolio.json"); d = pf.load_registry(p)
lane, order = "<lane>", ["<Name1>", "<Name2>"]   # Eric's order: active or paused rows only
for i, name in enumerate(order):
    row = board_ops.find(d, name)
    assert row["lane"] == lane and row["status"] in ("active", "paused"), name

input.prompt:
Research question for Baylor Football Applied Performance: which countermovement jump (CMJ) force-plate metrics best detect neuromuscular fatigue in college American football players, so staff can flag players for practice modification (report to position coaches) and modify Monday/Wednesday lifts? Context: testing is VALD ForceDecks, 2 CMJs hands-on-hips, during the lift warm-up, Monday (~48 h post-game) and Wednesday (~72 h pre-kickoff). The current draft decision tree uses three metrics with % drop from baseline: RSI-modified (Imp-Mom), jump height (Imp-Mom), contraction time; thresholds GREEN > -6.5%, AMBER -7 to -10% or CT +5-8%, RED > -10% or CT > +8% (Wednesday: -6/-11%). Note: the department's own readiness flag switched from RSI-mod to Peak Power / BM in July 2026.

Step 1 (required): invoke the Skill tool with skill "sports-science-research-grounding" and follow it. It searches Eric's Zotero library first (mcp__zotero__* tools; load them with ToolSearch first) and labels any external peer-reviewed sources. Good Zotero search terms: countermovement jump fatigue, neuromuscular fatigue, RSI modified, flight time contraction time, eccentric, football monitoring, post-match recovery, smallest worthwhile change, Claudino 2016 autoregulating jump performance, Anicic 2023 what should we report, Kruczek 2026 readiness preparedness bias, Gathercole, Cormack 2008, Taylor, Heishman, Bishop, Merrigan. External: use Firecrawl research tools (firecrawl_research_search_papers, load with ToolSearch) if Zotero is thin.

Answer, with citations (author, year, and whether it is in Zotero or external):
1. Which metrics are most sensitive to fatigue vs most reliable (CV%, ICC, SWC)? Rank: RSI-mod, jump height, flight time:contraction time, contraction time, eccentric duration, eccentric deceleration RFD / impulse, concentric impulse, peak power/BM, countermovement depth, mean force. Note "outcome vs strategy" (jump height can hold while strategy/timing metrics change).
2. Are the -6.5% / -10% thresholds defensible? What does the evidence say about using individual SWC / CV / z-scores vs fixed % cuts; rolling vs fixed baselines; how many reps (best vs mean of 2).
3. Evidence specific to American football (college or NFL) for post-game CMJ time course (24/48/72 h) and in-season monitoring.
4. Evidence that CMJ-guided load modification changes outcomes (performance, injury) vs just describing fatigue.
5. A recommended metric set for this tool: 1 primary outcome metric, 1-2 strategy metrics, with the reasoning, and what to drop.

Also read these local files for Baylor's OWN data (they are evidence; cite them): /Users/kristinarash/DEV/ForcePlate_DecisionSystem/docs/cmj_measurement_properties.md and /Users/kristinarash/DEV/ForcePlate_DecisionSystem/docs/readiness_metric_switch.md and /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Research/Flint/docs/synthesis/peaking-and-taper-in-season-football.md. Say where the literature and Baylor's numbers agree or conflict.

Save the full findings as Markdown at /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Football/Gemini_Projects/docs/research/cmj_fatigue_metrics_evidence.md (create the folder; do not commit). Return a compact summary (under 400 words): the ranked metrics, the threshold verdict, the recommended set, and the 3-5 most important citations. Read-only everywhere else; no athlete-identifiable data in the file.

# CMJ measurement properties in D1 football: what these metrics can and cannot see

**Status:** analysis complete
**Data:** 185 athletes, 92,550 athlete-metric-days, 5,930 retest pairs per metric, 2023–2025
**Reproduce:** `python -m src.research.measurement`

## Why this comes first

Ward's framing puts measurement ahead of modelling — validity, reliability,
responsiveness — because a metric that cannot resolve a meaningful change will
return a null regardless of how well the study is designed.

We arrived here the hard way. Six separate attempts to detect a practice-load
effect on readiness returned nothing. Before concluding that practice load has
no effect, we checked whether our instruments could have seen one.

## Method

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Typical error (TE)** | SD(difference) / √2 across consecutive **same-weekday** tests ≤10 days apart |
| **SWC** | 0.2 × between-athlete SD (conventional smallest worthwhile change) |
| **SWC / TE** | Below 1, the metric cannot resolve a worthwhile change even in principle |

Same-weekday pairing is deliberate. Monday and Thursday sit at different points
in the training week, so pooling them would charge real weekly rhythm to
measurement noise and overstate TE.

## Results

| Metric | TE % | SWC/TE | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Concentric Impulse | 2.9 | 0.99 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Peak Power / BM | 3.8 | 0.78 | cannot resolve SWC |
| P1 Concentric Impulse | 4.8 | 0.69 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Jump Height (Imp-Mom) | 5.7 | 0.63 | cannot resolve SWC |
| P2 Concentric Impulse | 6.3 | 0.57 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Concentric Impulse-100ms | 8.4 | 0.50 | cannot resolve SWC |
| **RSI-modified** | **8.8** | **0.48** | cannot resolve SWC |
| Eccentric Duration | 6.6 | 0.42 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Eccentric Deceleration RFD / BM | 18.4 | 0.42 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Eccentric Peak Power / BM | 13.4 | 0.34 | cannot resolve SWC |

**None of the ten metrics resolves the smallest worthwhile change at
individual, week-to-week resolution.**

## Two caveats, both of which make this less damning than it reads

1. **TE here is week-to-week typical variation, not instrument reliability.**
   It includes genuine biological fluctuation over up to 10 days. Same-session
   repeat-trial TE would be considerably smaller. What is reported is the right
   denominator for *weekly monitoring decisions* — which is the use case — but
   it should not be quoted as the reliability of the force plate.

2. **The 0.2 × SD convention is harsh in a homogeneous population.** D1
   football athletes within a position band are similar to each other, so the
   between-athlete SD is small, so the SWC is small. This is a known limitation
   of the convention in elite samples rather than a property of these metrics
   specifically.

Both caveats push in the same direction: the ratios above are pessimistic. The
practical conclusion survives anyway.

## What follows operationally

- **Do not act on a single athlete's single-week change.** In every metric, a
  one-week move is dominated by noise. This is the most important line in this
  document.
- **Trends across several tests are the usable unit**, which is an argument for
  denser, more regular testing rather than less. See
  `camp_2026_testing_ask.md`.
- **Stop defaulting to RSI-modified.** It is the field's habitual readiness
  metric and it carries **more than twice** the week-to-week noise of Peak
  Power / BM (8.8% vs 3.8%) in this population.
- **Peak Power / BM is the best headline metric**, on the reliability /
  responsiveness trade-off rather than on either alone. Concentric Impulse is
  quieter (TE 2.9%, ratio 0.99) but essentially inert — its mean Monday →
  Thursday change is +0.06%, so it is stable precisely because nothing moves
  it. Peak Power / BM is second-quietest and second-most responsive (+0.90%).

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project Overview

This is a decision support system for analyzing Countermovement Jump (CMJ) force plate data collected via **VALD ForceDecks** for **Football** athletes. It classifies athletes, diagnoses movement deficits, and drives training prescriptions throughout the competitive season.

**Status:** Implemented. Full pipeline built across 15 tasks. 120 tests passing across 9 test files. V3 dashboard with 5-tab layout, SSC/plyo staging, phase composites, microcycle prescriptions, and physio flags.

## Commands

```bash
python -m pytest -v                           # run all tests
python -m pytest tests/test_engine.py -v      # run a single test file
python run_pipeline.py --dry-run              # verify API auth, no DB writes
python run_pipeline.py                        # pull + classify + store
python run_pipeline.py --report               # pull + classify + HTML dashboard
python run_pipeline.py --report-only          # HTML dashboard from existing DB
python run_pipeline.py --reset-baseline <ID>  # reset one athlete's baseline
python run_pipeline.py --diagnose             # show all athletes and inclusion/exclusion reason
python run_pipeline.py --diagnose "Name"      # search for a specific athlete by name

# Multi-sport central store
python run_pipeline.py --sport-cmj Volleyball # ingest one sport's CMJ, no classification
python run_pipeline.py --reattribute          # fill name/sport/position from VALD roster
python run_pipeline.py --reattribute Volleyball --reset-sport

# Rep-level football CMJ: every rep, metric, limb -> cmj_trials (+ metric_definitions labels)
python run_pipeline.py --cmj-trials --from-date 2025-10-20 --recorded-from 2025-10-20 --recorded-to 2026-10-20
```

`raw_tests` keeps one rep (the first trial the API lists) and bilateral values only. `cmj_trials`
keeps all of them, in the unit named on each row; join `metric_definitions` on `result_id`, not name.

## The database is a multi-sport central store

`raw_tests` holds CMJ data for **every sport on the Baylor VALD tenant**, not just
football, and always has — `run_cmj_raw_backfill` pulls every CMJ test on the tenant and
only ever resolved *names* for football-rostered athletes. That is why 65% of rows
arrived with a blank `athlete_name`. Of 1.25M rows only ~163k are football.

`sport` (added 2026-08) makes that explicit. Attribution comes from
`reattribute_from_vald()`, which walks the VALD roster and fills in name, sport,
position and position group. After the first full run:

| sport | rows | athletes |
|---|---:|---:|
| (unattributed — profile deleted from tenant) | 374,232 | 231 |
| Archive | 328,961 | 317 |
| Football | 162,600 | 107 |
| Acrobatics and Tumbling | 100,417 | 50 |
| Volleyball | 43,216 | 18 |
| …15 more sports | | |

**Never backfill `sport` to 'Football'.** It is the obvious shortcut and it is wrong —
it relabels every other sport. NULL means "not yet attributed", which is honest and
lets a query decide. Other systems (e.g. `Kinexon_Volleyball`) read this database
read-only rather than keeping their own copy.

### Sport boundaries in the classification engine

`raw_tests` is sport-agnostic. `classified_athletes` is **football only** by
construction: the 4-step engine scores athletes against NFL normative percentiles keyed
by football position, and no equivalent normative table exists for volleyball.
`--sport-cmj` therefore stops at raw metrics. Anything built on a non-football sport
must compare an athlete to her own history, which needs no external norm.

## Scheduled pull and Parquet snapshots (Mac owns forceplate.db)

`data/forceplate.db` is a **DuckDB** file despite the `.db` name. The Mac is its only writer: launchd
`com.keystone.valdpull` runs `pull_vald.sh` (10:10 + 16:40). After a successful pipeline run it runs
`run_pipeline.py --reattribute` (~4 s; since 2026-10-29, so new tests get `sport`; exit in the receipt as
`reattribute_exit`, a failure alerts but never fails the pull). Then
`pull_vald.sh` runs `export_snapshot.py` (logic in `src/snapshot.py`), which opens the DB read-only and
writes Parquet to Google Drive for Windows and other read-only consumers:

- **Where:** `$ATHLETE_SNAPSHOT_DIR/vald/`, else `00_Primary_Storage_Drive/athlete-snapshots/vald/`
  (Mac `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My Drive/...`, Windows `G:\My Drive\...`).
  One file per table: `raw_tests` (all sports, ~12 MB), `classified_athletes`, `imtp_tests`,
  `athlete_baselines`, plus `manifest.json` (per table: rows, bytes, written_at UTC, machine, newest
  `test_date` / `baseline_date`). No table is skipped (there are no log tables); transient `_`-prefixed
  work tables such as `_vald_roster` are.
- **Windows reads, never writes:**
  `duckdb.sql("select * from 'G:/My Drive/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/athlete-snapshots/vald/raw_tests.parquet'")`.
- **Atomic:** written as `<table>.parquet.tmp`, then renamed.
- **Stale-writer guard:** a table whose snapshot already records more rows than this DB is refused
  (exit 3; the other tables are still written) unless `--force`. After `--reset-baseline` shrinks
  `athlete_baselines`, run `export_snapshot.py --force` by hand.
- **Failure:** exit 0 ok · 1 error · 2 no DB / Drive not mounted · 3 refused. Non-zero alerts
  (`snapshot-export exit=N`) and is recorded in `logs/last_run.json` under `snapshot_export`; the pull's
  exit code is unchanged. The export prints table names and counts only, never names.
- **By hand (Mac):** `.venv/bin/python export_snapshot.py --dry-run`, then without `--dry-run`.

## Project Structure

```
src/
  ingest/vald_client.py    # VALD ForceDecks API client (OAuth2 + REST)
  ingest/pipeline.py       # Data pull orchestration, football athlete filter
  classify/engine.py       # 4-step classification orchestrator
  classify/asymmetry.py    # Step 1: bilateral asymmetry screen
  classify/mrsi.py         # Step 2: mRSI tier classification
  classify/eccentric.py    # Step 3: eccentric profile confirmation
  classify/p1p2.py         # Step 4: concentric impulse quadrant
  report/html_dashboard.py # Jinja2 HTML report generator + SVG radar charts
  report/templates/dashboard.html.j2  # Dashboard Jinja2 template (Baylor branded)
  report/templates/dashboard.html.j2.bak  # Pre-redesign template backup
  db.py                    # DuckDB schema + queries
config/thresholds.yaml     # Position-specific normative percentiles
run_pipeline.py            # CLI entry point
```

## Domain Model: 4-Step Classification Pipeline

The core logic selects 42 metrics from 239 available in VALD ForceDecks:

**Step 1 — Asymmetry Screen** ([src/classify/asymmetry.py](src/classify/asymmetry.py))
Bilateral Asymmetry Braking Impulse: <10% pass, 10–15% caution, >15% flag (restrict + 48h clinical eval)

**Step 2 — mRSI Primary Classification** ([src/classify/mrsi.py](src/classify/mrsi.py))
mRSI vs position-specific P25/P75: ≥P75 → gold, ≥P25 → purple, <P25 → white

**Step 3 — Eccentric Profile Confirmation** ([src/classify/eccentric.py](src/classify/eccentric.py))
EPF/BM ≥2.5x AND peak_power_bm ≥P75 → gold_confirm; EPF/BM <2.0x → ecc_flag (downgrades gold→purple)

**Step 4 — P1/P2 Concentric Impulse Quadrant** ([src/classify/p1p2.py](src/classify/p1p2.py))
CI sorted into Q1–Q4 by position norms; P1/P2 sub-quadrant via 62%/38% proportional split of quartile midpoint

## Athlete Classification Tiers

| Tier | Threshold | Color |
|------|-----------|-------|
| Elite | ≥ P75 | GOLD |
| Average | P25–P75 | PURPLE |
| Developmental | < P25 | WHITE |

## Implementation Gotchas

- **HTML dashboard (V3)**: `--report` generates a single self-contained HTML file (`reports/YYYY-MM-DD_team_dashboard.html`) with 5 tabs: Overview (position-grouped roster), Profiles (radar + phase composite bars), Training Rx (MD-1–MD-4 microcycles + station groups), Plyo Stages (Wilmot continuum by SSC regime), Physio Flags (landing risk + localStorage notes). Baylor branding (#001a0d bg, #FECB00 accents). A persistent summary stats bar shows squad-wide tier/flag counts above all tabs. `team_name` is set to `"Baylor Football"` in `render_dashboard()`.
- **DuckDB SQL**: Use `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and `ON CONFLICT (pk) DO UPDATE SET excluded.*` — SQLite syntax (`INSERT OR IGNORE`, `INSERT OR REPLACE`) does not work
- **PyJWT 2.x**: `jwt.decode()` requires `algorithms=["RS256", "HS256"]` even when `verify_signature: False`
- **kaleido**: Pin `kaleido>=0.2,<1.0` — v1.x requires an external Chrome install; v0.x is self-contained
- **Readiness flags**: Consecutive logic (both tests must exceed threshold) is checked BEFORE single-test red (>10%) so the >15% consecutive-red path remains reachable
- **P1/P2 medians**: Derived dynamically from quartile CI boundaries (`ci_mid * 0.62` / `* 0.38`), not hardcoded global values
- **Eccentric metric split**: `Eccentric Peak Force / BM [N/kg]` is used for the 2.5x/2.0x EPF gates in Step 3; `Eccentric Peak Power / BM [W/kg]` is stored separately for display
- **Baseline management**: Dashboard trend compares current test vs average of first 4 tests in current season per athlete. Athletes with <4 tests show "Establishing baseline (N/4 tests)". Classification baselines (`athlete_baselines` table) set on first occurrence only; never auto-updated. Manual reset via CLI flags only.
- **Movement type units**: API returns Eccentric Duration in **seconds** (not ms) and Countermovement Depth as **negative cm**. `_movement_type()` uses `abs()` on depth and second-based thresholds (0.450s / 0.600s). Missing data shows "Unknown" instead of defaulting to "Balanced". Current thresholds produce a skewed distribution (~93% Balanced) — most fast athletes don't also go deep (>38cm), and most slow athletes still have moderate depth.
- **Template display conversions**: Eccentric Duration is stored in seconds but displayed as `× 1000` ms in the template. Countermovement Depth is stored as negative cm but displayed as `| abs |` positive cm. Bodyweight is stored in kg but displayed as `× 2.20462` lbs. These conversions happen in `dashboard.html.j2`, not in Python.
- **Movement strategy badges**: Color-coded by type in the template via `badge-move-{{ type | lower | replace(' ', '-') }}` classes — Balanced (green), Fast-Deep (cyan), Slow-Shallow (orange), Slow-Deep (purple), Unknown (gray).
- **Config path in classify modules**: Use `Path(__file__).parent.parent.parent / "config" / "thresholds.yaml"` — relative paths break when tests run from project root
- **Radar SVG layout**: 360×400 viewBox (width × height), radius 140. `_SVG_H = 400` gives room for both value labels and legend. Value labels use `_TWO_DECIMAL_KEYS` set for RSI-modified and FT:CT (2 decimal places); all others get 1 decimal place.
- **Position grouping**: `POSITION_ORDER` constant in `html_dashboard.py` controls roster group order. Filter JS hides empty position groups; sort operates within each `.card-grid`, not across groups.
- **Prescriptions schema (V3)**: `config/thresholds.yaml` prescriptions are now nested dicts keyed by `group → quadrant → {text, plyo_station, md4, md3, md2, md1}`. `p1p2.py` reads `prescriptions[group][quadrant]["text"]`. `html_dashboard.py` reads `md4`–`md1` and `plyo_station` from the same dict in `build_athlete_context()`. Old flat key format (`gold.low_p1: "..."`) is no longer valid.
- **SSC regime**: Computed in `html_dashboard.py::_ssc_regime()` from `Contraction Time` (seconds) using `ssc_thresholds` in `thresholds.yaml`. Fast SSC < 0.150s, Slow SSC > 0.250s, Mixed SSC in between. Falls back to "Unknown" when CT is missing.
- **Plyo staging**: `_plyo_stage(ssc, final_group, ci_quartile)` returns `(stage: int, locked: bool)`. Ceiling by SSC: Fast=5, Mixed=3, Slow=2. Stage bumped by CI quartile within ceiling. `locked=True` when stage ≥ 4 and SSC is not Fast.
- **Phase composites**: `_phase_composites()` returns 5 normalized delta dicts `{label, delta, positive}`. Delta = `(value - p50) / (p75 - p25)`, clamped to [-2, 2]. Landing composite is inverted (lower PLF/BM is better). Requires `ft_ct` and `plf_bm` thresholds in `thresholds.yaml` per position.
- **Physio flags**: `_physio_flags()` checks `plf_bm_flag`, `jh_rel_plf_flag`, and `asymmetry_braking.caution` per position. Returns list of `{label, value, threshold, exceeded}`. Physio notes saved to `localStorage` in browser, keyed by `physio_note_<athlete_id>`.
- **Encoding in thresholds.yaml**: All prescription text must use ASCII dashes (`-`), not en-dashes or em-dashes — non-ASCII dashes cause mojibake in browser rendering.
- **Stale deps**: `streamlit`, `plotly`, `xhtml2pdf` remain in `requirements.txt` but are unused after the move to pure Jinja2 HTML. Safe to remove.
- **Python 3.14**: Project runs on Python 3.14.0 — some packages may have compatibility warnings

## VALD API Gotchas

- **Team ID**: `4828f39e-7bb5-4178-8b25-1d9371fa9d09` (Baylor University) — use this exact UUID in `.env`, not the encoded `ZIEhQbmiBQkubFg==` string
- **Football filter**: Athletes have `attributes[typeName=="Sports"].valueName == "Football"` — 107 of 1,583 total athletes. Filter applied in `pipeline.py:is_football_athlete()`
- **Metric names**: No unit suffixes in API — `"RSI-modified"` not `"RSI-modified [m/s]"`, `"Eccentric Peak Force / BM"` not `"Eccentric Peak Force / BM [N/kg]"`, etc.
- **RSI-modified scale**: API returns value × 100 (e.g., 73.0 = 0.73 m/s). Apply `resultUnitScaleFactor = 0.01` from `/resultdefinitions`. Only factors < 1 are applied; time metrics (×1000 to ms) are left as-is since raw values are already in seconds. Duration metrics (Eccentric Duration, Concentric Duration, Contraction Time) are stored in **seconds** in `raw_tests`.
- **Asymmetry from bilateral trials**: Within a `limb="Both"` trial, each result has a `result.limb` field: `"Trial"` (combined), `"Left"`, `"Right"`, `"Asym"` (asymmetry %). Stored as `"Eccentric Braking Impulse Asymmetry"` key.
- **Result definitions endpoint**: `GET /resultdefinitions` → 512 metric definitions with `resultName`, `resultUnit`, `resultUnitScaleFactor`. Cached in `VALDClient.get_result_definitions()`.
- **Landing Stiffness**: API name is `"Landing Stiffness"` (confirmed via `/resultdefinitions`), `supportsAsymmetry: true`.
- **Per-test trials call**: One `GET /v2019q3/teams/{teamId}/tests/{testId}/trials` per test — 2,730 calls for 2026 season data takes ~8 minutes.

## Key Metrics (42 total)

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project Overview

This is a decision support system for analyzing Countermovement Jump (CMJ) force plate data collected via **VALD ForceDecks** for **Football** athletes. It classifies athletes, diagnoses movement deficits, and drives training prescriptions throughout the competitive season.

**Status:** Implemented. Full pipeline built across 15 tasks. 120 tests passing across 9 test files. V3 dashboard with 5-tab layout, SSC/plyo staging, phase composites, microcycle prescriptions, and physio flags.

## Commands

```bash
python -m pytest -v                           # run all tests
python -m pytest tests/test_engine.py -v      # run a single test file
python run_pipeline.py --dry-run              # verify API auth, no DB writes
python run_pipeline.py                        # pull + classify + store
python run_pipeline.py --report               # pull + classify + HTML dashboard
python run_pipeline.py --report-only          # HTML dashboard from existing DB
python run_pipeline.py --reset-baseline <ID>  # reset one athlete's baseline
python run_pipeline.py --diagnose             # show all athletes and inclusion/exclusion reason
python run_pipeline.py --diagnose "Name"      # search for a specific athlete by name

# Multi-sport central store
python run_pipeline.py --sport-cmj Volleyball # ingest one sport's CMJ, no classification
python run_pipeline.py --reattribute          # fill name/sport/position from VALD roster
python run_pipeline.py --reattribute Volleyball --reset-sport

# Rep-level football CMJ: every rep, metric, limb -> cmj_trials (+ metric_definitions labels)
python run_pipeline.py --cmj-trials --from-date 2025-10-20 --recorded-from 2025-10-20 --recorded-to 2026-10-20
```

`raw_tests` keeps one rep (the first trial the API lists) and bilateral values only. `cmj_trials`
keeps all of them, in the unit named on each row; join `metric_definitions` on `result_id`, not name.

## The database is a multi-sport central store

`raw_tests` holds CMJ data for **every sport on the Baylor VALD tenant**, not just
football, and always has — `run_cmj_raw_backfill` pulls every CMJ test on the tenant and
only ever resolved *names* for football-rostered athletes. That is why 65% of rows
arrived with a blank `athlete_name`. Of 1.25M rows only ~163k are football.

`sport` (added 2026-08) makes that explicit. Attribution comes from
`reattribute_from_vald()`, which walks the VALD roster and fills in name, sport,
position and position group. After the first full run:

| sport | rows | athletes |
|---|---:|---:|
| (unattributed — profile deleted from tenant) | 374,232 | 231 |
| Archive | 328,961 | 317 |
| Football | 162,600 | 107 |
| Acrobatics and Tumbling | 100,417 | 50 |
| Volleyball | 43,216 | 18 |
| …15 more sports | | |

**Never backfill `sport` to 'Football'.** It is the obvious shortcut and it is wrong —
it relabels every other sport. NULL means "not yet attributed", which is honest and
lets a query decide. Other systems (e.g. `Kinexon_Volleyball`) read this database
read-only rather than keeping their own copy.

### Sport boundaries in the classification engine

`raw_tests` is sport-agnostic. `classified_athletes` is **football only** by
construction: the 4-step engine scores athletes against NFL normative percentiles keyed
by football position, and no equivalent normative table exists for volleyball.
`--sport-cmj` therefore stops at raw metrics. Anything built on a non-football sport
must compare an athlete to her own history, which needs no external norm.

## Scheduled pull and Parquet snapshots (Mac owns forceplate.db)

`data/forceplate.db` is a **DuckDB** file despite the `.db` name. The Mac is its only writer: launchd
`com.keystone.valdpull` runs `pull_vald.sh` (10:10 + 16:40). After a successful pipeline run it runs
`run_pipeline.py --reattribute` (~4 s; since 2026-10-29, so new tests get `sport`; exit in the receipt as
`reattribute_exit`, a failure alerts but never fails the pull). Then
`pull_vald.sh` runs `export_snapshot.py` (logic in `src/snapshot.py`), which opens the DB read-only and
writes Parquet to Google Drive for Windows and other read-only consumers:

- **Where:** `$ATHLETE_SNAPSHOT_DIR/vald/`, else `00_Primary_Storage_Drive/athlete-snapshots/vald/`
  (Mac `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My Drive/...`, Windows `G:\My Drive\...`).
  One file per table: `raw_tests` (all sports, ~12 MB), `classified_athletes`, `imtp_tests`,
  `athlete_baselines`, plus `manifest.json` (per table: rows, bytes, written_at UTC, machine, newest
  `test_date` / `baseline_date`). No table is skipped (there are no log tables); transient `_`-prefixed
  work tables such as `_vald_roster` are.
- **Windows reads, never writes:**
  `duckdb.sql("select * from 'G:/My Drive/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/athlete-snapshots/vald/raw_tests.parquet'")`.
- **Atomic:** written as `<table>.parquet.tmp`, then renamed.
- **Stale-writer guard:** a table whose snapshot already records more rows than this DB is refused
  (exit 3; the other tables are still written) unless `--force`. After `--reset-baseline` shrinks
  `athlete_baselines`, run `export_snapshot.py --force` by hand.
- **Failure:** exit 0 ok · 1 error · 2 no DB / Drive not mounted · 3 refused. Non-zero alerts
  (`snapshot-export exit=N`) and is recorded in `logs/last_run.json` under `snapshot_export`; the pull's
  exit code is unchanged. The export prints table names and counts only, never names.
- **By hand (Mac):** `.venv/bin/python export_snapshot.py --dry-run`, then without `--dry-run`.

```
src/
  ingest/vald_client.py    # VALD ForceDecks API client (OAuth2 + REST)
  ingest/pipeline.py       # Data pull orchestration, football athlete filter
  classify/engine.py       # 4-step classification orchestrator
  classify/asymmetry.py    # Step 1: bilateral asymmetry screen
  classify/mrsi.py         # Step 2: mRSI tier classification
  classify/eccentric.py    # Step 3: eccentric profile confirmation
  classify/p1p2.py         # Step 4: concentric impulse quadrant
  report/html_dashboard.py # Jinja2 HTML report generator + SVG radar charts

The core logic selects 42 metrics from 239 available in VALD ForceDecks:

**Step 1 — Asymmetry Screen** ([src/classify/asymmetry.py](src/classify/asymmetry.py))
Bilateral Asymmetry Braking Impulse: <10% pass, 10–15% caution, >15% flag (restrict + 48h clinical eval)

**Step 2 — mRSI Primary Classification** ([src/classify/mrsi.py](src/classify/mrsi.py))
mRSI vs position-specific P25/P75: ≥P75 → gold, ≥P25 → purple, <P25 → white

**Step 3 — Eccentric Profile Confirmation** ([src/classify/eccentric.py](src/classify/eccentric.py))
EPF/BM ≥2.5x AND peak_power_bm ≥P75 → gold_confirm; EPF/BM <2.0x → ecc_flag (downgrades gold→purple)

**Step 4 — P1/P2 Concentric Impulse Quadrant** ([src/classify/p1p2.py](src/classify/p1p2.py))
CI sorted into Q1–Q4 by position norms; P1/P2 sub-quadrant via 62%/38% proportional split of quartile midpoint

| Tier | Threshold | Color |
|------|-----------|-------|

# CMJ measurement properties in D1 football: what these metrics can and cannot see

**Status:** analysis complete
**Data:** 185 athletes, 92,550 athlete-metric-days, 5,930 retest pairs per metric, 2023–2025
**Reproduce:** `python -m src.research.measurement`

## Why this comes first

Ward's framing puts measurement ahead of modelling — validity, reliability,
responsiveness — because a metric that cannot resolve a meaningful change will
return a null regardless of how well the study is designed.

We arrived here the hard way. Six separate attempts to detect a practice-load
effect on readiness returned nothing. Before concluding that practice load has
no effect, we checked whether our instruments could have seen one.

## Method

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Typical error (TE)** | SD(difference) / √2 across consecutive **same-weekday** tests ≤10 days apart |
| **SWC** | 0.2 × between-athlete SD (conventional smallest worthwhile change) |
| **SWC / TE** | Below 1, the metric cannot resolve a worthwhile change even in principle |

Same-weekday pairing is deliberate. Monday and Thursday sit at different points
in the training week, so pooling them would charge real weekly rhythm to
measurement noise and overstate TE.

## Results

| Metric | TE % | SWC/TE | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Concentric Impulse | 2.9 | 0.99 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Peak Power / BM | 3.8 | 0.78 | cannot resolve SWC |
| P1 Concentric Impulse | 4.8 | 0.69 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Jump Height (Imp-Mom) | 5.7 | 0.63 | cannot resolve SWC |
| P2 Concentric Impulse | 6.3 | 0.57 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Concentric Impulse-100ms | 8.4 | 0.50 | cannot resolve SWC |
| **RSI-modified** | **8.8** | **0.48** | cannot resolve SWC |
| Eccentric Duration | 6.6 | 0.42 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Eccentric Deceleration RFD / BM | 18.4 | 0.42 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Eccentric Peak Power / BM | 13.4 | 0.34 | cannot resolve SWC |

**None of the ten metrics resolves the smallest worthwhile change at
individual, week-to-week resolution.**

## Two caveats, both of which make this less damning than it reads

1. **TE here is week-to-week typical variation, not instrument reliability.**
   It includes genuine biological fluctuation over up to 10 days. Same-session
   repeat-trial TE would be considerably smaller. What is reported is the right
   denominator for *weekly monitoring decisions* — which is the use case — but
   it should not be quoted as the reliability of the force plate.

2. **The 0.2 × SD convention is harsh in a homogeneous population.** D1
   football athletes within a position band are similar to each other, so the
   between-athlete SD is small, so the SWC is small. This is a known limitation
   of the convention in elite samples rather than a property of these metrics
   specifically.

Both caveats push in the same direction: the ratios above are pessimistic. The
practical conclusion survives anyway.

## What follows operationally

- **Do not act on a single athlete's single-week change.** In every metric, a
  one-week move is dominated by noise. This is the most important line in this
  document.
- **Trends across several tests are the usable unit**, which is an argument for
  denser, more regular testing rather than less. See
  `camp_2026_testing_ask.md`.
- **Stop defaulting to RSI-modified.** It is the field's habitual readiness
  metric and it carries **more than twice** the week-to-week noise of Peak
  Power / BM (8.8% vs 3.8%) in this population.
- **Peak Power / BM is the best headline metric**, on the reliability /
  responsiveness trade-off rather than on either alone. Concentric Impulse is
  quieter (TE 2.9%, ratio 0.99) but essentially inert — its mean Monday →
  Thursday change is +0.06%, so it is stable precisely because nothing moves
  it. Peak Power / BM is second-quietest and second-most responsive (+0.90%).

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project Overview

This is a decision support system for analyzing Countermovement Jump (CMJ) force plate data collected via **VALD ForceDecks** for **Football** athletes. It classifies athletes, diagnoses movement deficits, and drives training prescriptions throughout the competitive season.

**Status:** Implemented. Full pipeline built across 15 tasks. 120 tests passing across 9 test files. V3 dashboard with 5-tab layout, SSC/plyo staging, phase composites, microcycle prescriptions, and physio flags.

## Commands

```bash
python -m pytest -v                           # run all tests
python -m pytest tests/test_engine.py -v      # run a single test file
python run_pipeline.py --dry-run              # verify API auth, no DB writes
python run_pipeline.py                        # pull + classify + store
python run_pipeline.py --report               # pull + classify + HTML dashboard
python run_pipeline.py --report-only          # HTML dashboard from existing DB
python run_pipeline.py --reset-baseline <ID>  # reset one athlete's baseline
python run_pipeline.py --diagnose             # show all athletes and inclusion/exclusion reason
python run_pipeline.py --diagnose "Name"      # search for a specific athlete by name

# Multi-sport central store
python run_pipeline.py --sport-cmj Volleyball # ingest one sport's CMJ, no classification
python run_pipeline.py --reattribute          # fill name/sport/position from VALD roster
python run_pipeline.py --reattribute Volleyball --reset-sport

# Rep-level football CMJ: every rep, metric, limb -> cmj_trials (+ metric_definitions labels)
python run_pipeline.py --cmj-trials --from-date 2025-10-20 --recorded-from 2025-10-20 --recorded-to 2026-10-20
```

`raw_tests` keeps one rep (the first trial the API lists) and bilateral values only. `cmj_trials`
keeps all of them, in the unit named on each row; join `metric_definitions` on `result_id`, not name.

## The database is a multi-sport central store

`raw_tests` holds CMJ data for **every sport on the Baylor VALD tenant**, not just
football, and always has — `run_cmj_raw_backfill` pulls every CMJ test on the tenant and
only ever resolved *names* for football-rostered athletes. That is why 65% of rows
arrived with a blank `athlete_name`. Of 1.25M rows only ~163k are football.

`sport` (added 2026-08) makes that explicit. Attribution comes from
`reattribute_from_vald()`, which walks the VALD roster and fills in name, sport,
position and position group. After the first full run:

| sport | rows | athletes |
|---|---:|---:|
| (unattributed — profile deleted from tenant) | 374,232 | 231 |
| Archive | 328,961 | 317 |
| Football | 162,600 | 107 |
| Acrobatics and Tumbling | 100,417 | 50 |
| Volleyball | 43,216 | 18 |
| …15 more sports | | |

**Never backfill `sport` to 'Football'.** It is the obvious shortcut and it is wrong —
it relabels every other sport. NULL means "not yet attributed", which is honest and
lets a query decide. Other systems (e.g. `Kinexon_Volleyball`) read this database
read-only rather than keeping their own copy.

### Sport boundaries in the classification engine

`raw_tests` is sport-agnostic. `classified_athletes` is **football only** by
construction: the 4-step engine scores athletes against NFL normative percentiles keyed
by football position, and no equivalent normative table exists for volleyball.
`--sport-cmj` therefore stops at raw metrics. Anything built on a non-football sport
must compare an athlete to her own history, which needs no external norm.

## Scheduled pull and Parquet snapshots (Mac owns forceplate.db)

`data/forceplate.db` is a **DuckDB** file despite the `.db` name. The Mac is its only writer: launchd
`com.keystone.valdpull` runs `pull_vald.sh` (10:10 + 16:40). After a successful pipeline run it runs
`run_pipeline.py --reattribute` (~4 s; since 2026-10-29, so new tests get `sport`; exit in the receipt as
`reattribute_exit`, a failure alerts but never fails the pull). Then
`pull_vald.sh` runs `export_snapshot.py` (logic in `src/snapshot.py`), which opens the DB read-only and
writes Parquet to Google Drive for Windows and other read-only consumers:

- **Where:** `$ATHLETE_SNAPSHOT_DIR/vald/`, else `00_Primary_Storage_Drive/athlete-snapshots/vald/`
  (Mac `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My Drive/...`, Windows `G:\My Drive\...`).
  One file per table: `raw_tests` (all sports, ~12 MB), `classified_athletes`, `imtp_tests`,
  `athlete_baselines`, plus `manifest.json` (per table: rows, bytes, written_at UTC, machine, newest
  `test_date` / `baseline_date`). No table is skipped (there are no log tables); transient `_`-prefixed
  work tables such as `_vald_roster` are.
- **Windows reads, never writes:**
  `duckdb.sql("select * from 'G:/My Drive/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/athlete-snapshots/vald/raw_tests.parquet'")`.
- **Atomic:** written as `<table>.parquet.tmp`, then renamed.
- **Stale-writer guard:** a table whose snapshot already records more rows than this DB is refused
  (exit 3; the other tables are still written) unless `--force`. After `--reset-baseline` shrinks
  `athlete_baselines`, run `export_snapshot.py --force` by hand.
- **Failure:** exit 0 ok · 1 error · 2 no DB / Drive not mounted · 3 refused. Non-zero alerts
  (`snapshot-export exit=N`) and is recorded in `logs/last_run.json` under `snapshot_export`; the pull's
  exit code is unchanged. The export prints table names and counts only, never names.
- **By hand (Mac):** `.venv/bin/python export_snapshot.py --dry-run`, then without `--dry-run`.

## Project Structure

```
src/
  ingest/vald_client.py    # VALD ForceDecks API client (OAuth2 + REST)
  ingest/pipeline.py       # Data pull orchestration, football athlete filter
  classify/engine.py       # 4-step classification orchestrator
  classify/asymmetry.py    # Step 1: bilateral asymmetry screen
  classify/mrsi.py         # Step 2: mRSI tier classification
  classify/eccentric.py    # Step 3: eccentric profile confirmation
  classify/p1p2.py         # Step 4: concentric impulse quadrant
  report/html_dashboard.py # Jinja2 HTML report generator + SVG radar charts
  report/templates/dashboard.html.j2  # Dashboard Jinja2 template (Baylor branded)
  report/templates/dashboard.html.j2.bak  # Pre-redesign template backup
  db.py                    # DuckDB schema + queries
config/thresholds.yaml     # Position-specific normative percentiles
run_pipeline.py            # CLI entry point
```

## Domain Model: 4-Step Classification Pipeline

The core logic selects 42 metrics from 239 available in VALD ForceDecks:

**Step 1 — Asymmetry Screen** ([src/classify/asymmetry.py](src/classify/asymmetry.py))
Bilateral Asymmetry Braking Impulse: <10% pass, 10–15% caution, >15% flag (restrict + 48h clinical eval)

**Step 2 — mRSI Primary Classification** ([src/classify/mrsi.py](src/classify/mrsi.py))
mRSI vs position-specific P25/P75: ≥P75 → gold, ≥P25 → purple, <P25 → white

**Step 3 — Eccentric Profile Confirmation** ([src/classify/eccentric.py](src/classify/eccentric.py))
EPF/BM ≥2.5x AND peak_power_bm ≥P75 → gold_confirm; EPF/BM <2.0x → ecc_flag (downgrades gold→purple)

**Step 4 — P1/P2 Concentric Impulse Quadrant** ([src/classify/p1p2.py](src/classify/p1p2.py))
CI sorted into Q1–Q4 by position norms; P1/P2 sub-quadrant via 62%/38% proportional split of quartile midpoint

## Athlete Classification Tiers

| Tier | Threshold | Color |
|------|-----------|-------|
| Elite | ≥ P75 | GOLD |
| Average | P25–P75 | PURPLE |
| Developmental | < P25 | WHITE |

## Implementation Gotchas

- **HTML dashboard (V3)**: `--report` generates a single self-contained HTML file (`reports/YYYY-MM-DD_team_dashboard.html`) with 5 tabs: Overview (position-grouped roster), Profiles (radar + phase composite bars), Training Rx (MD-1–MD-4 microcycles + station groups), Plyo Stages (Wilmot continuum by SSC regime), Physio Flags (landing risk + localStorage notes). Baylor branding (#001a0d bg, #FECB00 accents). A persistent summary stats bar shows squad-wide tier/flag counts above all tabs. `team_name` is set to `"Baylor Football"` in `render_dashboard()`.
- **DuckDB SQL**: Use `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and `ON CONFLICT (pk) DO UPDATE SET excluded.*` — SQLite syntax (`INSERT OR IGNORE`, `INSERT OR REPLACE`) does not work
- **PyJWT 2.x**: `jwt.decode()` requires `algorithms=["RS256", "HS256"]` even when `verify_signature: False`
- **kaleido**: Pin `kaleido>=0.2,<1.0` — v1.x requires an external Chrome install; v0.x is self-contained
- **Readiness flags**: Consecutive logic (both tests must exceed threshold) is checked BEFORE single-test red (>10%) so the >15% consecutive-red path remains reachable
- **P1/P2 medians**: Derived dynamically from quartile CI boundaries (`ci_mid * 0.62` / `* 0.38`), not hardcoded global values
- **Eccentric metric split**: `Eccentric Peak Force / BM [N/kg]` is used for the 2.5x/2.0x EPF gates in Step 3; `Eccentric Peak Power / BM [W/kg]` is stored separately for display
- **Baseline management**: Dashboard trend compares current test vs average of first 4 tests in current season per athlete. Athletes with <4 tests show "Establishing baseline (N/4 tests)". Classification baselines (`athlete_baselines` table) set on first occurrence only; never auto-updated. Manual reset via CLI flags only.
- **Movement type units**: API returns Eccentric Duration in **seconds** (not ms) and Countermovement Depth as **negative cm**. `_movement_type()` uses `abs()` on depth and second-based thresholds (0.450s / 0.600s). Missing data shows "Unknown" instead of defaulting to "Balanced". Current thresholds produce a skewed distribution (~93% Balanced) — most fast athletes don't also go deep (>38cm), and most slow athletes still have moderate depth.
- **Template display conversions**: Eccentric Duration is stored in seconds but displayed as `× 1000` ms in the template. Countermovement Depth is stored as negative cm but displayed as `| abs |` positive cm. Bodyweight is stored in kg but displayed as `× 2.20462` lbs. These conversions happen in `dashboard.html.j2`, not in Python.
- **Movement strategy badges**: Color-coded by type in the template via `badge-move-{{ type | lower | replace(' ', '-') }}` classes — Balanced (green), Fast-Deep (cyan), Slow-Shallow (orange), Slow-Deep (purple), Unknown (gray).
- **Config path in classify modules**: Use `Path(__file__).parent.parent.parent / "config" / "thresholds.yaml"` — relative paths break when tests run from project root
- **Radar SVG layout**: 360×400 viewBox (width × height), radius 140. `_SVG_H = 400` gives room for both value labels and legend. Value labels use `_TWO_DECIMAL_KEYS` set for RSI-modified and FT:CT (2 decimal places); all others get 1 decimal place.
- **Position grouping**: `POSITION_ORDER` constant in `html_dashboard.py` controls roster group order. Filter JS hides empty position groups; sort operates within each `.card-grid`, not across groups.
- **Prescriptions schema (V3)**: `config/thresholds.yaml` prescriptions are now nested dicts keyed by `group → quadrant → {text, plyo_station, md4, md3, md2, md1}`. `p1p2.py` reads `prescriptions[group][quadrant]["text"]`. `html_dashboard.py` reads `md4`–`md1` and `plyo_station` from the same dict in `build_athlete_context()`. Old flat key format (`gold.low_p1: "..."`) is no longer valid.
- **SSC regime**: Computed in `html_dashboard.py::_ssc_regime()` from `Contraction Time` (seconds) using `ssc_thresholds` in `thresholds.yaml`. Fast SSC < 0.150s, Slow SSC > 0.250s, Mixed SSC in between. Falls back to "Unknown" when CT is missing.
- **Plyo staging**: `_plyo_stage(ssc, final_group, ci_quartile)` returns `(stage: int, locked: bool)`. Ceiling by SSC: Fast=5, Mixed=3, Slow=2. Stage bumped by CI quartile within ceiling. `locked=True` when stage ≥ 4 and SSC is not Fast.
- **Phase composites**: `_phase_composites()` returns 5 normalized delta dicts `{label, delta, positive}`. Delta = `(value - p50) / (p75 - p25)`, clamped to [-2, 2]. Landing composite is inverted (lower PLF/BM is better). Requires `ft_ct` and `plf_bm` thresholds in `thresholds.yaml` per position.
- **Physio flags**: `_physio_flags()` checks `plf_bm_flag`, `jh_rel_plf_flag`, and `asymmetry_braking.caution` per position. Returns list of `{label, value, threshold, exceeded}`. Physio notes saved to `localStorage` in browser, keyed by `physio_note_<athlete_id>`.
- **Encoding in thresholds.yaml**: All prescription text must use ASCII dashes (`-`), not en-dashes or em-dashes — non-ASCII dashes cause mojibake in browser rendering.
- **Stale deps**: `streamlit`, `plotly`, `xhtml2pdf` remain in `requirements.txt` but are unused after the move to pure Jinja2 HTML. Safe to remove.
- **Python 3.14**: Project runs on Python 3.14.0 — some packages may have compatibility warnings

## VALD API Gotchas

- **Team ID**: `4828f39e-7bb5-4178-8b25-1d9371fa9d09` (Baylor University) — use this exact UUID in `.env`, not the encoded `ZIEhQbmiBQkubFg==` string
- **Football filter**: Athletes have `attributes[typeName=="Sports"].valueName == "Football"` — 107 of 1,583 total athletes. Filter applied in `pipeline.py:is_football_athlete()`
- **Metric names**: No unit suffixes in API — `"RSI-modified"` not `"RSI-modified [m/s]"`, `"Eccentric Peak Force / BM"` not `"Eccentric Peak Force / BM [N/kg]"`, etc.
- **RSI-modified scale**: API returns value × 100 (e.g., 73.0 = 0.73 m/s). Apply `resultUnitScaleFactor = 0.01` from `/resultdefinitions`. Only factors < 1 are applied; time metrics (×1000 to ms) are left as-is since raw values are already in seconds. Duration metrics (Eccentric Duration, Concentric Duration, Contraction Time) are stored in **seconds** in `raw_tests`.
- **Asymmetry from bilateral trials**: Within a `limb="Both"` trial, each result has a `result.limb` field: `"Trial"` (combined), `"Left"`, `"Right"`, `"Asym"` (asymmetry %). Stored as `"Eccentric Braking Impulse Asymmetry"` key.
- **Result definitions endpoint**: `GET /resultdefinitions` → 512 metric definitions with `resultName`, `resultUnit`, `resultUnitScaleFactor`. Cached in `VALDClient.get_result_definitions()`.
- **Landing Stiffness**: API name is `"Landing Stiffness"` (confirmed via `/resultdefinitions`), `supportsAsymmetry: true`.
- **Per-test trials call**: One `GET /v2019q3/teams/{teamId}/tests/{testId}/trials` per test — 2,730 calls for 2026 season data takes ~8 minutes.

## Key Metrics (42 total)

**Tier 1 — Performance Outputs (3 metrics)**
- Jump Height, RSI-modified, Flight Time:Contraction Time

**Tier 2 — Braking Phase (5 metrics)**
- ECC Deceleration RFD (`EDRFD/BM` — most sensitive metric for deceleration injury risk)

**Tier 2 — Propulsive Phase (10 metrics)**

- Concentric RFD, Concentric RFD @100ms, P1/P2 Concentric Impulse, P2:P1 Ratio, Con Mean Force/BM

**Tier 2 — Landing Phase (6 metrics)**
- Peak Landing Force, Peak Landing Force/BM, JH-Relative Peak Landing Force
- Landing RFD, Landing RFD 50ms, Landing Stiffness

**Tier 3 — Movement Strategy (9 metrics)**
- Eccentric Duration, Concentric Duration, Countermovement Depth
- ECC:CON Duration Ratio, ECC:CON Mean Force Ratio, ECC:CON Peak Power Ratio
- Contraction Time, CMJ Stiffness, Lower-Limb Stiffness

**Metadata (1):** Body Mass

## Primary Decision Thresholds (NFL Normative Percentiles by Position)

All thresholds are in `config/thresholds.yaml` keyed by full position name. Each position gets its own P25/P50/P75 — not a pooled group average.

**P1/P2 Concentric Impulse Quartile boundaries (per position):**
- Q1: 0 → q1_max | Q2: q1_max → q2_max | Q3: q2_max → q3_max | Q4: q3_max → q3_max×1.15

## Stakeholder Hierarchy (Tactical Hierarchy of Injury Mitigation)

Controls ~90% of fatigue via training design (dose controllers):
1. **Technical Staff** (High control) — duration, pitch size, session intensity, match minutes
2. **Sports Scientist** (Medium control) — GPS/HR data interpretation, load monitoring
3. **S&C Coach** (Medium control) — tissue tolerance via eccentric loading, plyometrics
4. **Medical Staff** (Low control) — reactive; screening, inflammation management

## Football-Specific Normative Data (Fully Available)

The VALD 2024-25 NFL and NCAA Football Report provides P5/P25/P50/P75/P95 values for all CMJ metrics across 10 positions for both NFL and NCAA athletes:

**Positions covered:** Defensive Back, Defensive Line, Linebacker, Offensive Line, Quarterback, Running Back, Tight End, Wide Receiver, Special Teams, Kicker/Punter

**Position group mapping for classification:**
- `skill`: DB, LB, QB, RB, WR, TE, ST, K/P
- `big`: DL, OL

**Key NFL medians for reference (skill positions):**
| Metric | DB | WR | RB | LB |
|--------|----|----|----|----|
| Jump Height Imp-Mom (cm) | 47.9 | 48.0 | 45.5 | 43.7 |
| RSI-Modified (m/s) | 0.74 | 0.74 | 0.69 | 0.66 |
| FT:CT | 0.94 | 0.94 | 0.90 | 0.87 |
| Peak Power/BM (W/kg) | 67.4 | 67.5 | 64.5 | 61.3 |
| EDRFD/BM (N/s/kg) | 119 | 116 | 114 | 108 |
| Ecc Peak Power/BM (W/kg) | 24.1 | 23.6 | 22.4 | 23.8 |

**Key NFL medians for reference (big positions):**
| Metric | OL | DL |
|--------|----|----|
| Jump Height Imp-Mom (cm) | 33.1 | 37.7 |
| RSI-Modified (m/s) | 0.47 | 0.56 |
| Peak Power/BM (W/kg) | 49.7 | 55.1 |
| EDRFD/BM (N/s/kg) | 74 | 89 |

## Documentation

- [`docs/coaches_manual.md`](docs/coaches_manual.md) — V3 user manual: 5-tab dashboard navigation, classification interpretation, SSC/plyo staging guide, and role-specific best-use workflows
- [`docs/coaches_manual_v1.md`](docs/coaches_manual_v1.md) — Original (pre-V3) manual preserved for reference

## Reference Documents

All reference materials are in [`ContextBackgroundInfo/`](ContextBackgroundInfo/):

- [`CMJ Force Plate Thresholding-Pentheny.pdf`](ContextBackgroundInfo/CMJ%20Force%20Plate%20Thresholding-Pentheny.pdf) — Primary threshold framework, GOLD/PURPLE/WHITE classification system

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/plugins/cache/mattpocock/mattpocock-skills/1.3.2/skills/productivity/grilling

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
